title: The Glass and the Sentence: Galileo Galilei from Pisa to Arcetri
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pisa, the parish of Sant'Andrea: the birth
stops.date_confidence: Date and city attested (Museo Galileo, Galileo's Life chronology: born February 15 in Pisa), as are the parents and his rank as eldest child. The house is not. The baptismal register places the family in the chapel of Sant'Andrea and the pin follows that; the traditional address in the Chiasso dei Mercanti, some three hundred metres west, was settled on only in the late nineteenth century and is local tradition, not document.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of February a first child is born to Vincenzo Galilei, lutenist and music theorist, and to Giulia Ammannati of Pescia. Vincenzo is at this moment arguing in print against the numerology of his own teacher, insisting that the ratios of consonance be settled by stretched strings and hung weights rather than by the authority of Pythagoras. Five more children follow. The baptismal register, which puts the household in the chapel of Sant'Andrea, is the only document that places the family anywhere in the city that February.
suggested_refs: The Pisan baptismal register entry locating the Galilei household in Chapella di S.to Andrea
Vincenzo Galilei, Dialogo della musica antica et della moderna (Florence, 1581)
sources: Italian Wikipedia, 'Galileo Galilei', on the disputed birth house

stops.name: Pisa, the Baptistery: the name given
stops.date_confidence: Attested; Museo Galileo chronology. Coordinate corrected to the Baptistery's own position, 43.72333 N, 10.39389 E.
stops.campa: Four days after the birth he is carried across the city to the round baptistery on the Piazza dei Miracoli and christened Galileo Galilei, the given name repeating the family name in the Tuscan manner for a first son. The building is a drum of white marble known for its acoustics: a note sung under the dome comes back some seconds later as a chord. It stands a hundred paces from the cathedral whose hanging lamp he will be said, twenty years on, to have timed against the beat of his own pulse.
suggested_refs: The Battistero di San Giovanni, Piazza dei Miracoli, Pisa

stops.name: Florence: the family follows the lute trade
stops.date_confidence: Year disputed and left unresolved: MacTutor gives 1572 for the move, with Galileo left behind in Pisa with a relative and joining at about ten; the Museo Galileo chronology gives 1574. Dated here to 1574; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: Vincenzo moves the household to Florence, where the Camerata is remaking Italian music and a theorist can be paid for an opinion. The boy does not travel with them at once; he is left behind in Pisa with a relative and joins the family after. In Florence his father is at work on the Dialogo della musica antica et della moderna, reporting experiments on strings loaded with weights, measuring where the ear says an interval ought to fall and finding the Pythagorean numbers wrong about it.
suggested_refs: Vincenzo Galilei's string-and-weight experiments, described in the Dialogo of 1581

stops.name: Badia di Vallombrosa: the boy who wanted to stay
stops.date_confidence: Schooling dated c.1575-1578; month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. The novitiate and the eye inflammation given as the pretext for his removal descend from Vincenzo Viviani's Racconto istorico of 1654 and are tradition, not document. MacTutor calls the house Camaldolese; it is Vallombrosan, the mother house of the order.
stops.campa: Thirty kilometres southeast of Florence, in beech forest on the flank of the Pratomagno, the Vallombrosan monks take him as a pupil. He learns Latin and Greek and the ordinary logic of the schools, and likes the life well enough to enter the community as a novice. Vincenzo, informed that his eldest son proposes to give himself to a religious order instead of to a paying profession, comes up the mountain and removes him, citing an inflammation of the boy's eyes. Whether the eyes were inflamed is recorded nowhere but in Viviani, writing seventy years later.
suggested_refs: Vincenzo Viviani, Racconto istorico della vita di Galileo (1654; printed 1717)
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Vallombrosa Abbey', coordinates and order

stops.name: University of Pisa: enrolled for medicine, taught Euclid
stops.date_confidence: Matriculation attested to 5 September 1580 (Museo Galileo). The Ricci course is dated by MacTutor to the academic year 1582-83 at Pisa, with a further meeting at Florence in the summer of 1583; the dossier's placement of the Euclid encounter at the Florentine court is wrong and is corrected here to Pisa.
stops.campa: On the fifth of September he matriculates in the Faculty of Arts to read medicine, the career his father has chosen for him because physicians are paid and mathematicians are not. In the academic year 1582 to 1583 Ostilio Ricci, mathematician to the Tuscan court, teaches a course on Euclid's Elements at the university; Galileo attends it, and afterwards will not go back to medicine. Ricci meets him again in Florence the next summer and takes his side against Vincenzo. Four and a half years later he leaves Pisa with no degree at all.
suggested_refs: Ostilio Ricci's Euclid course at Pisa, academic year 1582-83

stops.name: Pisa Cathedral, the nave: the lamp and the pulse
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, not document. Museo Galileo and MacTutor both give the observation under 1583, but nothing in Galileo's hand from that year records it; his earliest surviving statement of pendulum isochronism is the 1602 letter to Guidobaldo del Monte, nineteen years later. Month and day unknown and defaulted. Strict isochronism holds only for small arcs.
stops.campa: The story told of him in these student years is set in the nave, under the great hanging lamp: that he watches it swing after a sacristan has pulled it aside to light it, times the swings against the beat of his own wrist, and finds that a wide swing and a narrow one take the same interval. Nothing survives in his hand from 1583 to say that it happened. The earliest writing in which he sets out the isochronism of the pendulum is a letter of 1602 to Guidobaldo del Monte, and the isochronism itself is only approximate.
suggested_refs: Galileo to Guidobaldo del Monte, 29 November 1602, on the equal times of unequal swings

stops.name: Siena: lessons for hire
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1585-1586 by MacTutor; the month is an ordering device only and the day is defaulted.
stops.campa: Out of the university with nothing on paper to show for four and a half years, he goes back to Florence and then on to Siena, where he takes private pupils in mathematics and holds a public teaching appointment. He is twenty-one, unqualified, and supporting himself by the subject his father forbade him. Between lessons he works through Archimedes, whom he will go on describing for the rest of his life as the only ancient worth arguing from. Applications for a proper chair at Bologna and elsewhere come back refused.
suggested_refs: Galileo's Sienese teaching appointment, 1585-1586

stops.name: Florence: La bilancetta
stops.date_confidence: Composition attested to 1586; month and day unknown and defaulted. The tract circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1644, two years after his death.
stops.campa: In his father's house he writes a short tract, La bilancetta, on the hydrostatic balance: a reconstruction of how Archimedes must actually have tested the crown of Hiero, done with a beam, a fine wire wound close on one arm, and a weighing in water, rather than with the overflowing bath of the anecdote. The bath makes a story; the wire and the beam make a measurement another man can repeat. Copies go out in manuscript to anyone who might employ him. The tract is not printed until 1644.
suggested_refs: La bilancetta, Italian text and English translation, math.nyu.edu/Archimedes/Crown/bilancetta.html
sources: NYU digitized text of La bilancetta

stops.name: Collegio Romano: an audience with Clavius
stops.date_confidence: Journey attested to 1587 (MacTutor: in the following year he travelled to Rome to visit Clavius); month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the Collegio Romano itself, Piazza del Collegio Romano, 41.8980861 N, 12.4802611 E.
stops.campa: He travels to Rome to put his work before Christopher Clavius, the Jesuit mathematician of the Collegio Romano, the architect of the calendar reform that had taken ten days out of October five years earlier, and the man whose good opinion opens mathematical chairs across Italy. Clavius receives him; the two correspond afterwards on centres of gravity in solids. Nothing comes of the visit at once. The chairs he applies for go to other men, and he goes home to Florence with a correspondence and no post.
suggested_refs: The Galileo-Clavius correspondence on centres of gravity, 1587-1588

stops.name: University of Pisa: the Dante lectures and the chair
stops.date_confidence: Both attested: the Accademia Fiorentina lectures on Dante to 1588 (MacTutor), the inaugural address at Pisa to 12 November 1589 with teaching beginning two days later (Museo Galileo). The geography lens gave the Dante lectures as 1587-1588; the chronology and MacTutor both give 1588, and 1588 is used.
stops.campa: An invitation from the Accademia Fiorentina the year before had him lecture on the size, site, and shape of Dante's Inferno, measuring the cone of hell in Florentine braccia and reasoning about whether a vault of that span could stand. The performance is noticed by men who make appointments. In November 1589 he takes up the chair of mathematics at Pisa, reads his inaugural address on the twelfth and begins teaching on the fourteenth, at a salary a fraction of what the professors of philosophy and medicine draw. He stays three years.
suggested_refs: Due lezioni all'Accademia Fiorentina circa la figura, sito e grandezza dell'Inferno di Dante (1588)

stops.name: The Leaning Tower of Pisa: the unequal weights
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, and disputed. The story rests solely on Viviani's account, written some sixty-five years after the fact from the recollection of an old and blind man. Galileo's own writings never mention the tower. Traditionally placed in his Pisan professorship, 1589-1592; the year here is an ordering device and the month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: The tradition is precise and unsupported: that he carried balls of unequal weight up the campanile, dropped them before the assembled professors of the university, and showed them striking the ground together, refuting Aristotle in front of witnesses. Viviani writes it down some sixty-five years later, from what an old blind man told a young assistant. Galileo's own books never mention the tower at all, and where he does describe dropping a cannonball beside a musket ball he reports that the heavier one arrives a little ahead.
suggested_refs: Physics World, 'The legend of the leaning tower'
Viviani, Racconto istorico della vita di Galileo (1654)

stops.name: Padua, Palazzo del Bo: the Venetian chair
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Venetian Senate appointment 26 September 1592, first lecture 7 December (Museo Galileo gives teaching beginning 13 December; MacTutor gives the inaugural lecture on 7 December, and the discrepancy is left standing). Vincenzo Galilei's death is attested to 1591 without a day in the reachable sources. The 1593 Campanella meeting is staged in tommaso_campanella.journey.json, not in Galileo's own documents.
stops.campa: His father dead the year before and a household of dependants left on him, he leaves Tuscany for the Venetian Republic, where a professor may say more and is paid better for it. The Senate appoints him in September; he lectures for the first time in December. The same chair had been sought, and refused, by Giordano Bruno, who was arrested in Venice that spring. In 1593 Tommaso Campanella passes through Padua and meets the new professor. Galileo holds the post eighteen years and afterwards calls them the happiest of his life.
suggested_refs: giordano_bruno.journey.json, on the Padua chair Bruno sought and did not get
tommaso_campanella.journey.json, on the 1593 Padua meeting

stops.name: Venice: the patent for raising water
stops.date_confidence: Patent attested to 1594 with a twenty-year term and a three-hundred-ducat penalty (Rice University Galileo Project, patent text). Month and day unknown and defaulted. The Arsenal is a standing relationship across the Padua years, not a dated visit, and is described here rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: Padua and Venice are a few hours apart by boat and he is often at the far end of the journey, in the Arsenal among shipwrights and gunfounders and the glassmen of Murano, asking the sort of question the university does not set; the Discorsi opens in that Arsenal forty years later. The Republic grants him a twenty-year privilege on a machine for raising water and irrigating land, worked by one horse and discharging through twenty spouts, with a penalty of three hundred ducats against anyone who copies it.
suggested_refs: The 1594 Venetian patent text, galileo.library.rice.edu/sci/instruments/pump.html
The Arsenale di Venezia, the workshop culture behind the Discorsi
sources: Rice University Galileo Project, patent text

stops.name: Padua: the compass, the workshop, and a letter to Prague
stops.date_confidence: Both the compass and the opening of the Kepler correspondence are attested to 1597; month and day unknown and defaulted. Kepler was at Graz in 1597 and moved to Prague in 1600, and the correspondence continues from there.
stops.campa: He designs a geometric and military compass, a brass sector engraved with scales that will do proportion, currency conversion, gunner's elevation, and the extraction of roots without any arithmetic. In the same year he writes for the first time to Johannes Kepler, tells him he has held the Copernican opinion for years, and adds that he does not publish it. A workshop goes up in his own house, where the instrument maker Marc'Antonio Mazzoleni turns the sectors out to order and the buyers pay again for the lessons that teach them the scales.
suggested_refs: Surviving Galilean sectors by Marc'Antonio Mazzoleni, Museo Galileo
johannes_kepler.journey.json

stops.name: San Lorenzo, Padua: the children of Marina Gamba
stops.date_confidence: Births attested: Virginia 13 August 1600, Livia 18 August 1601, Vincenzo 21 August 1606 (Museo Galileo). The stop is pinned at the parish church of San Lorenzo where the children were baptized; the precise footprint of the period church is approximate.
stops.campa: Virginia is baptized at the parish church on the thirteenth of August, daughter of Marina Gamba of Venice, who keeps a house nearby and whom Galileo does not marry. Livia follows in 1601, Vincenzo in 1606. Being illegitimate the daughters are held unmarriageable, and both will be placed as girls in the convent of San Matteo at Arcetri; the boy is legitimated later by grand-ducal decree. Virginia, in religion Suor Maria Celeste, becomes the person her father writes to most often and trusts furthest.
suggested_refs: The 124 surviving letters of Suor Maria Celeste to her father, galileo.library.rice.edu

stops.name: Padua: the Capra affair
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1607; month and day unknown and defaulted. The dossier's claim that the Difesa appeared the following year is corrected: Capra's tract, the rectors' judgment, and Galileo's Difesa all fall in 1607, the Difesa published at Venice.
stops.campa: In 1606 he prints Le operazioni del compasso geometrico et militare, the first book to carry his name, in an edition small enough to give away to the buyers of his instruments. The next year a former pupil, Baldessar Capra, publishes the same device in Latin as his own invention. Galileo takes him before the university's reformers, wins, watches the edition confiscated, and then, not satisfied with winning, publishes at Venice the Difesa contro alle calunnie et imposture di Baldessar Capra.
suggested_refs: Difesa contro alle calunnie et imposture di Baldessar Capra (Venice, 1607)
Paolo Rossini, 'Replicating Mathematical Inventions: Galileo's...', Perspectives on Science 30:3

stops.name: Campanile di San Marco: the Senate looks through the tube
stops.date_confidence: August 1609 attested for the demonstration and the Senate's reward of tenure and a raised salary; the twenty-first is the conventional day and MacTutor dates the spyglass letter to May 1609 with the demonstration following within months. Power of the instrument given variously as eight or nine.
stops.campa: Word reaches Venice of a Dutch device that makes distant things appear near. Working from the report alone and grinding his own lenses, within weeks he has an instrument better than the original, then better again. On the twenty-first of August he brings the Venetian Senate up the bell tower of St Mark's and lets the procurators look, one after another, at ships still two hours out at sea. The Republic confirms him for life and doubles his salary. He does not mention what he intends to point it at.
suggested_refs: Library of Congress essay on Galileo and the telescope
The two surviving Galilean telescopes, Museo Galileo, Florence
sources: Library of Congress, Galileo and the telescope

stops.name: Padua, his own house: four points around Jupiter
stops.date_confidence: Nights of 7 to 13 January 1610 attested (Museo Galileo). The exact address of the Padua house is not given in the reachable sources; the coordinate approximates the university quarter where he lodged. Kepler's Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo and the following year's Dioptrice are attested and are recorded on Kepler's own file.
stops.campa: From the seventh to the thirteenth of January he watches three, then four small lights strung near Jupiter, and establishes that they are not fixed stars: they change their places from night to night and never leave the planet behind. He works out that they go round it. In Prague, without an instrument of his own, Johannes Kepler reads the report and publishes his support within weeks. In the dedication Galileo names the four the Medicean Stars, for Cosimo II and his three brothers.
stops.quote: I therefore concluded and decided unhesitatingly, that there are three stars in the heavens moving about Jupiter, as Venus and Mercury round the Sun; which at length was established as clear as daylight by numerous subsequent observations.
stops.quote_source: Galileo, Sidereus Nuncius (1610), trans. Edward Stafford Carlos (1880), p. 47
suggested_refs: johannes_kepler.journey.json, on the Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo and the Dioptrice
Galileo's observation notebook for January 1610, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Florence

stops.name: Venice: Sidereus nuncius
stops.date_confidence: Museo Galileo dates the publication to 12 March 1610, English Wikipedia to 13 March, MacTutor to May; the discrepancy is left standing and 13 March used. Edition of about 550 copies, printed at Venice by Thomas Baglioni.
stops.campa: Five hundred and fifty copies in Latin, printed at Venice in March and sold out at once: a mountainous, cratered Moon drawn in wash from the ragged line of the terminator, the Milky Way resolved into separate stars, and the four moons of Jupiter offered to Cosimo II as the Medicean Stars. The book is twenty-four leaves long, and what it shows of the Moon is a surface with mountains and hollows on it. In Bologna and in Padua, professors of philosophy decline to put an eye to the tube at all.
stops.quote: My dear Kepler, what would you say of the learned here, who, replete with the pertinacity of the asp, have steadfastly refused to cast a glance through the telescope? What shall we make of this? Shall we laugh, or shall we cry?
suggested_refs: Sidereus nuncius (Venice: Thomas Baglioni, 1610), first edition

stops.name: Palazzo Pitti, Florence: philosopher to the Grand Duke
stops.date_confidence: Sequence corrected against the dossier: he resigned Padua in June 1610, signed with the Medici in July, and did not reach Florence until September. Day within September unknown and defaulted. The phases of Venus are attested to the autumn of 1610. MacTutor's phrasing Chief Mathematician at the University of Pisa is misleading; the post carried no teaching duty.
stops.campa: He resigns Padua in June, signs with the Medici in July, and arrives in Florence in September as Philosopher and Chief Mathematician to Cosimo II, salaried, with no teaching duty and with the title philosopher he had insisted on having in writing. Marina Gamba does not come; the daughters do, to the convent. The Venetians are not gracious about the departure. That autumn he watches Venus run through the whole cycle of phases a moon runs through. No arrangement centred on the earth can produce that. The one Tycho Brahe proposed can.
suggested_refs: The Medici appointment contract of July 1610
The phases of Venus as evidence against Ptolemy, still compatible with the Tychonic arrangement

stops.name: Collegio Romano: the Jesuits check the sky
stops.date_confidence: Spring 1611 attested (MacTutor, Museo Galileo); day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the Collegio Romano itself, 41.8980861 N, 12.4802611 E, replacing the dossier's 12.4823 which repeats across three Roman stops.
stops.campa: He comes to Rome with his telescopes and is received as a celebrity. The mathematicians of the Collegio Romano, Clavius among them, turn their own instruments on Jupiter and on Venus and confirm what he has reported, while reserving judgement about what any of it means. The college holds a public ceremony in his honour. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, separately and in writing, asks those same mathematicians whether the observations are sound, and they answer that they are. What the observations oblige a man to believe is a question nobody at the ceremony puts.
suggested_refs: Bellarmine's 1611 query to the mathematicians of the Collegio Romano and their reply

stops.name: Accademia dei Lincei: Galileo Galilei Linceo
stops.date_confidence: Admission attested to 25 April 1611. The pin is Federico Cesi's Roman palace in Borgo, where the Lincei operated in 1611; the dossier's 41.9036/12.465 appears to be a transposition, and the Academy's modern seat at Palazzo Corsini, 41.89333/12.46667, postdates Galileo by centuries. The banquet at which Giovanni Demisiani coined telescopio is attested to that spring in Rome; its precise venue could not be confirmed.
stops.campa: Federico Cesi, marchese of Monticelli, who at eighteen had founded an academy of four young men sworn to natural philosophy and named it for the lynx, admits him as its sixth member on the twenty-fifth of April. At a banquet held for him that spring the Greek theologian Giovanni Demisiani supplies the new instrument with a name, telescopio, far-seer. From this point he signs himself Galileo Galilei Linceo, and the Lincei will publish, finance, and defend his books until Cesi dies in 1630 and the academy dies with him.
suggested_refs: The Lincean imprint on the Istoria delle macchie solari (1613) and Il Saggiatore (1623)

stops.name: Rome: the letters on sunspots
stops.date_confidence: Publication attested to March 1613 under Lincean auspices; day unknown and defaulted. Pinned at Cesi's Roman establishment, which financed and issued the book, rather than at a printing house whose address is not in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: The Lincei print the Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle macchie solari e loro accidenti, three letters to the Augsburg magistrate Mark Welser, engraved with the spots crossing the disc day after day. Galileo argues that they are on the sun itself, carried round by its rotation, and that the sun is therefore not incorruptible either. The Jesuit Christoph Scheiner, writing under the name Apelles, had seen them independently and published first, and the two men argue about priority for ten years.
suggested_refs: Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle macchie solari (Rome: Accademia dei Lincei, 1613)
Christoph Scheiner, Tres epistolae de maculis solaribus (1612)

segments.name: Scripture, and the Qualifiers of the Holy Office

stops.name: Florence: the letter to Castelli
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 21 December 1613. The dinner conversation that prompted it took place at the Medici table with Castelli present; Galileo was not there. The letter circulated in manuscript and a copy of it reached the Holy Office in 1615.
stops.campa: At the grand-ducal table the Dowager Grand Duchess Christina had asked whether the motion of the earth does not contradict Scripture, and Benedetto Castelli, Galileo's pupil and a Benedictine, had answered as well as he could and then written to his teacher about it. Galileo replies on the twenty-first of December, and goes further than the dinner did: Scripture and nature proceed alike from God, Scripture accommodates its language to ordinary understanding, and a demonstrated natural conclusion cannot be overturned by a verse. Copies circulate, and one of them reaches the Holy Office two years later in a wording not quite his own.
suggested_refs: The Letter to Castelli, 21 December 1613, and the altered copy submitted to the Holy Office in 1615
sources: Rice University Galileo Project, documentary sources on the Castelli letter

stops.name: Santa Maria Novella: Caccini in the pulpit
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 21 December 1614 by the Museo Galileo chronology; the geography lens hedged 20-21 December and the chronology is followed. Coordinate corrected to the church itself, 43.7746 N, 11.2493 E. Galileo was not present: the stop records the pulpit from which the accusation against him was launched, not a scene he witnessed.
stops.campa: On the fourth Sunday of Advent the Dominican Tommaso Caccini preaches in the Florentine church on the text of Joshua commanding the sun to stand still, and takes the occasion to denounce mathematicians as a class, the doctrine of the moving earth, and Galileo close enough by name. Galileo is not in the congregation. Caccini's own superiors apologise privately. Within fifteen months Caccini is in Rome giving sworn testimony to the Holy Office, and it is the deposition, not the sermon, that opens the file on him.
suggested_refs: Caccini's deposition to the Holy Office, Rome, 20 March 1615

stops.name: Florence: the Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina
stops.date_confidence: Composition attested to 1615; month and day unknown and defaulted. The letter circulated only in manuscript in his lifetime and was first printed in 1636. The famous line about how one goes to heaven is quoted by Galileo from an unnamed ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree; the attribution to Cardinal Cesare Baronio is a later editorial identification and is not in the text.
stops.campa: He rewrites the Castelli letter at four times the length and addresses it to Christina of Lorraine herself: forty pages arguing from Augustine that where a demonstration is genuine, the theologian's business is to find the reading of Scripture that agrees with it, because the Holy Spirit did not set out to teach astronomy. It is the most carefully built thing he ever writes and he never publishes it. Manuscript copies go round Florence and Rome for twenty-one years, until it is printed in 1636, abroad, out of reach.
stops.quote: That the intention of the Holy Ghost is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes.
stops.quote_source: Galileo, Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615), quoting an unnamed ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree; English translation, sourcebooks.fordham.edu
suggested_refs: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina, first printed Strasbourg, 1636
sources: sourcebooks.fordham.edu, 'Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina'

stops.name: Palace of the Holy Office, Rome: the qualifiers report
stops.date_confidence: Sequence corrected against the dossier, which slid it a day late: 19 February the propositions are referred to the theological qualifiers, 24 February the qualifiers report, 25 February the Pope instructs Bellarmine, 26 February Bellarmine admonishes Galileo. The quote's wording comes from the 1633 indictment reciting the 1616 censure; the direct 1616 report is conventionally rendered foolish and absurd in philosophy, and formally heretical.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of February the Holy Office refers two propositions to its theological consultants: that the sun is the centre of the world and immovable, and that the earth is not the centre and moves with a daily motion. On the twenty-fourth the qualifiers report. The first proposition they call absurd and formally heretical; the second at least erroneous in the faith. The report names no one. Galileo is in Rome while they write, lobbying cardinals and lending out telescopes. The report is not shown to him.
stops.quote: The proposition that the sun is in the center of the world and immovable from its place is absurd, philosophically false, and formally heretical
stops.quote_source: Indictment of Galileo (1633), reciting the censure of the Theological Qualifiers; English translation, sourcebooks.fordham.edu
suggested_refs: The 1616 documentary file, transcribed at douglasallchin.net/galileo/library/1616docs.htm
sources: sourcebooks.fordham.edu, 'The Crime of Galileo: Indictment and Abjuration of 1633'

stops.name: Rome: Bellarmine's admonition
stops.date_confidence: Date attested to 26 February 1616. The venue is not: the admonition took place at Bellarmine's own residence, and the pin here follows the Jesuit quarter of the Collegio Romano with the coordinate corrected to 41.8981/12.4803. The discrepancy between the unsigned minute in the file and the certificate Bellarmine wrote out for Galileo on 26 May 1616 is real, unresolved in the record, and became the hinge of the 1633 prosecution.
stops.campa: Bellarmine sends for him and tells him, in the presence of a notary and witnesses of the Holy Office, that the Copernican opinion is to be abandoned. What exactly was said becomes the whole later question. An unsigned minute in the file records a stricter injunction, not to hold, teach, or defend the doctrine in any way whatsoever. The certificate Bellarmine writes out for him in his own hand three months later, at Galileo's request, says only that the doctrine has been declared contrary to Scripture and may not be held or defended. He keeps the paper. The two documents do not say the same thing, and the file does not explain why.
suggested_refs: Bellarmine's certificate to Galileo, 26 May 1616
The unsigned precept of 26 February 1616 in the Holy Office file

stops.name: Rome: the Index suspends Copernicus
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 5 March 1616. Campanella's Apologia pro Galileo is attested as written in 1616 in the prison of Castel Sant'Elmo and printed at Frankfurt in 1622; that stop belongs to Campanella and is on his own file, and is cited here as a relation, not staged as a scene.
stops.campa: The Congregation of the Index publishes its decree. De revolutionibus orbium coelestium by Nicolaus Copernicus, seventy-three years in print and dedicated to a pope, is suspended until corrected; Foscarini's book reconciling it with Scripture is prohibited outright. Galileo is not named anywhere in the decree, which is precisely what he will get Bellarmine to certify. In a cell of Castel Sant'Elmo above Naples, Tommaso Campanella is at that moment writing an Apologia pro Galileo that will not reach a press for six years.
suggested_refs: nicolaus_copernicus.journey.json
tommaso_campanella.journey.json, the Castel Sant'Elmo stop for the Apologia pro Galileo

stops.name: Florence: the three comets
stops.date_confidence: The comets of 1618 are attested; the month here orders the segment and the day is defaulted. Galileo's authorship of the Discorso published under Mario Guiducci's name is attested as substantial but not total. Grassi's parallax argument placing the comets beyond the moon was correct and Galileo's counter-argument was not.
stops.campa: Three comets appear in the autumn, and at the Collegio Romano the Jesuit Orazio Grassi measures their parallax and puts them beyond the moon, which is where they are. Galileo, ill in bed at Bellosguardo, will not have it, and answers through his pupil Mario Guiducci with a Discorso delle comete that he largely writes himself, arguing that comets are optical effects of vapours risen from the earth. Grassi has the better measurement and the better argument. Galileo answers him for six more years.
suggested_refs: Mario Guiducci, Discorso delle comete (Florence, 1619)
Orazio Grassi, De tribus cometis anni 1618 (Rome, 1619)

stops.name: Rome: Il Saggiatore
stops.date_confidence: Publication attested to 1623 at Rome under Lincean auspices, with the dedication to the newly elected Urban VIII added while the book was at press; month and day unknown, the month used as an ordering device. Pinned at the Lincean establishment that financed and issued it.
stops.campa: The Lincei print his reply to Grassi as Il Saggiatore, the assayer: a book about a comet that is really a book about how a claim gets weighed, written in Italian rather than Latin, and quotable in nearly every paragraph. While it is at press, Maffeo Barberini, who had taken Galileo's side eleven years earlier in an argument about floating bodies and written a poem in his honour, is elected Pope Urban VIII. The Lincei add a dedication to him. The new pope has the book read aloud to him at table.
stops.quote: Philosophy is written in this grand book, I mean the Universe, which stands continually open to our gaze, but it cannot be understood unless one first learns to comprehend the language and interpret the characters in which it is written. It is written in the language of mathematics, and its characters are triangles, circles, and other geometrical figures, without which it is humanly impossible to understand a single word of it; without these, one is wandering around in a dark labyrinth.
stops.quote_source: Galileo, Il Saggiatore (1623), trans. Stillman Drake, Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (1957), pp. 237-8. Drake's text uses a dash where a comma stands here; the wording is otherwise verbatim.
suggested_refs: Il Saggiatore (Rome: Giacomo Mascardi for the Accademia dei Lincei, 1623)

stops.name: The Vatican: six audiences with Urban VIII
stops.date_confidence: Six audiences in 1624 are given by the documentary biographies (Fantoli, Finocchiaro) synthesized in the dossier; the Museo Galileo chronology independently dates a papal audience with a microscope demonstration to 10 May 1624, and that day is used to order the stop. The precise chamber is not established. Urban's argument about divine omnipotence is attested and reappears in the mouth of Simplicio in 1632.
stops.campa: He comes to Rome in the spring to congratulate the new pope and is granted six audiences in six weeks, along with a painting, two medals, a pension for his son, and a letter of praise addressed to the Grand Duke. He demonstrates a compound microscope. What he is not granted is permission. Urban tells him the doctrine may be handled as a hypothesis, since God being omnipotent could produce the same appearances by means beyond human imagining, and that this argument must be given its place in anything he writes. He goes home and starts the Dialogue.
suggested_refs: Museo Galileo on the 1624 papal audience and the microscope

stops.name: Florence: the Dialogo goes to press
stops.date_confidence: Publication attested to 22 February 1632 at Florence. The licensing history, split between the Roman and Florentine censors and interrupted by plague quarantine on the roads, is attested; the exact terms agreed at each stage are contested in the scholarship and are not adjudicated here.
stops.campa: Two years of licensing between Rome and Florence, plague quarantine shutting the roads between them, an imprimatur negotiated twice, a preface required and duly supplied. The book comes out on the twenty-second of February: three speakers across four days, Salviati arguing for Copernicus, Sagredo the intelligent listener, and Simplicio holding the Aristotelian line and given, in the closing pages, Urban's own argument about divine omnipotence to deliver. The Ptolemaic case is spoken by a character whose name means simpleton. In August, seven months after publication, the sale is stopped.
suggested_refs: Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo (Florence: Landini, 1632)

stops.name: Palazzo Firenze, Rome: lodging with the ambassador
stops.date_confidence: Summons attested to 1 October 1632; arrival in Rome attested to February 1633, conventionally the thirteenth. The quarantine delay at the Tuscan border and the pleas of ill health are attested; the reported threat to bring him in chains is standard in the biographies and is not re-verified against the original correspondence here.
stops.campa: Summoned in October, he pleads age and sickness through the winter and is told that if he will not come of his own accord he will be fetched in irons. He is sixty-eight. He travels by litter, sits twenty-two days in quarantine at the Tuscan border because of plague, and reaches Rome in the middle of February, lodging at the Palazzo Firenze with the Tuscan ambassador Francesco Niccolini, who has orders from his Grand Duke to house him well and keep him quiet. Nobody questions him until April.
suggested_refs: Niccolini's dispatches to Florence during Galileo's stay at Palazzo Firenze

stops.name: Palace of the Holy Office: the first interrogation
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 12 April 1633. The comfortable conditions of his detention, rooms of a tribunal official with a servant and food from the embassy, are attested. Whether the unsigned 1616 precept was validly served remains unresolved in the scholarship and is not adjudicated here.
stops.campa: He crosses the Tiber to the Inquisition's palace beside St Peter's and is lodged inside it, not in a cell but in the rooms of one of the tribunal's own officials, with a servant and meals sent over from the embassy. The interrogation turns entirely on 1616 and on what Bellarmine had said to him. He produces the certificate in Bellarmine's hand. The file produces the unsigned minute with the stricter wording. Bellarmine has been dead twelve years. Asked whether the Dialogue defends the condemned opinion, he answers that it refutes it.
suggested_refs: The interrogation transcripts of April to June 1633, Vatican Archives
sources: Museo Galileo, 'Sentence and Condemnation of Galileo' (catalogue.museogalileo.it)

stops.name: Santa Maria sopra Minerva: the abjuration
stops.date_confidence: Date and sentence text attested (Museo Galileo). On 21 June he had been formally threatened with rigorous examination, the judicial preliminary to torture; nothing in the record shows torture was administered. The Minerva convent as venue is standard identification but is not named in the sentence document itself. The tradition that he then muttered Eppur si muove first appears in print in Giuseppe Baretti's The Italian Library, London 1757, one hundred and twenty-four years later; it is absent from the trial record, from his correspondence, and from Viviani's biography, and is carried here as legend only. Pin inherited from tommaso_campanella.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the great hall of the Dominican convent, kneeling before the assembled cardinals of the Holy Office, he hears the sentence read out: vehemently suspected of heresy, the Dialogue prohibited, formal imprisonment at the pleasure of the tribunal, the seven penitential psalms to be recited weekly for three years. Then, still kneeling, from a text set in front of him, he abjures, curses, and detests the opinion that the earth moves. Seven of the ten cardinals put their names to the sentence. The other three do not.
stops.quote: you have rendered yourself in the judgment of this Holy Office vehemently suspected of heresy
stops.quote_source: Sentence of the Inquisition against Galileo, 22 June 1633, English translation, Museo Galileo
suggested_refs: Galileo's Abjuration, 22 June 1633: with sincere heart and unfeigned faith I abjure, curse, and detest the aforesaid errors and heresies
Giuseppe Baretti, The Italian Library (London, 1757), first print appearance of Eppur si muove
tommaso_campanella.journey.json, which abjured de vehementi in this same nave in 1595
sources: Museo Galileo, 'Sentence and Condemnation of Galileo'

stops.name: Siena, the Archbishop's palace: a gentler custody
stops.date_confidence: The Siena custody under Archbishop Ascanio Piccolomini is attested to July-December 1633; the day within July is an ordering device. The intermediate stay at the Villa Medici in Rome, attested to late June, is described here rather than given a pin of its own. The anonymous denunciations sent to Rome about Piccolomini's table talk are attested in the Holy Office file.
stops.campa: The prison sentence is commuted the day after it is handed down. He is held first at the Villa Medici on the Pincio under the Grand Duke's protection, then permitted, on Tuscan petition, to go to Siena into the custody of Archbishop Ascanio Piccolomini, who admires him. Piccolomini gives him a room, invites the learned of the city to dinner to meet him, and encourages him to write again. Unsigned reports reach Rome complaining that the archbishop is telling his guests Galileo was condemned unjustly. The custody at Siena lasts five months.
suggested_refs: The anonymous denunciations of Piccolomini in the Holy Office file, 1633

stops.name: Villa Il Gioiello, Arcetri: home, under guard
stops.date_confidence: Return attested to 1 December 1633 (Museo Galileo). Coordinate corrected to via del Pian dei Giullari 42, 43.7476 N, 11.2576 E; the dossier's 43.7519/11.2461 and the afterlife lens's 43.75917/11.2425 are both wrong and are not used. Descartes's withdrawal of Le Monde on hearing of the condemnation is attested in his correspondence with Mersenne and is staged on his own file at Deventer, not here.
stops.campa: On the first of December he is let back into the house he had taken on the hillside below Florence, on the Pian dei Giullari, a few hundred metres from the convent where both his daughters live. The terms are set out: he may not leave it, may not entertain visitors in numbers, may not discuss the motion of the earth with anyone. In the Dutch Republic that same winter, hearing what Rome has done, Rene Descartes takes Le Monde back from his printer.
suggested_refs: rene_descartes.journey.json, the Deventer stop where the news of the condemnation reaches him
Villa Il Gioiello, via del Pian dei Giullari 42, Arcetri

stops.name: Convent of San Matteo, Arcetri: the death of Suor Maria Celeste
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 2 April 1634. The 124 surviving letters and the fact that his own side of the correspondence does not survive are attested through the Rice University Galileo Project, which the dossier names as its documentary basis and which was not re-fetched in this pass; the underlying dates are corroborated by Museo Galileo.
stops.campa: Suor Maria Celeste, born Virginia at Padua, thirty-three years old, placed here at thirteen because an illegitimate daughter could not be married off, has spent the four months since his return running his household correspondence and his medicines and, at his own request, reciting his weekly penitential psalms in his place. She falls ill with dysentery and is dead within days. A hundred and twenty-four of her letters to him survive. His side of the correspondence does not survive at all.
suggested_refs: The letters of Suor Maria Celeste, galileo.library.rice.edu/fam/daughter.html
sources: Rice University Galileo Project (cited via the dossier, not re-fetched)

stops.name: Costa San Giorgio, Florence: a blind man allowed a city
stops.date_confidence: February 1638 attested (Museo Galileo); the day is defaulted. The cause of the blindness is undetermined in the medical-history literature, cataract and glaucoma both being proposed. The inquisitor's phrase is quoted from the Museo Galileo chronology's rendering of his February 1638 report to Rome.
stops.campa: Blind for about two years, from cataract or glaucoma or something the physicians of the age had no name for, he petitions to be allowed into Florence for treatment. An earlier request of the same kind had been answered with the threat of an actual prison. The Florentine inquisitor sends Rome his own assessment of the petitioner's state. The request is granted on conditions: a house on the Costa San Giorgio close to his son's, no visitors, no conversation about the motion of the earth.
stops.quote: more a cadaver than a living person
stops.quote_source: Report of the Florentine inquisitor to Rome, February 1638, quoted in the Museo Galileo chronology
suggested_refs: Medical-history review of Galileo's blindness, adsabs.harvard.edu/full/2011ASPC..441...73T

stops.name: Leiden: the Discorsi printed out of reach
stops.date_confidence: Publication attested to July 1638, printed by the Elzevirs at Leiden; day unknown and defaulted. That the manuscript left Italy past the censorship is attested; the precise route and the identity of every carrier are not established in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: The manuscript leaves Italy in pieces, carried out by friends, and comes together at the Elzevir press in Leiden, in a republic where the Roman Index has no force. Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze returns the four speakers of the Dialogue to subjects nobody has forbidden: why a beam of a given shape snaps at a given length, why a giant's own bones would fail him, how far a falling body travels in the second second and in the third. A copy is sent to him at Arcetri. He cannot read it.
suggested_refs: Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze (Leiden: Elzevir, 1638)

stops.name: Villa Il Gioiello: the last pupils
stops.date_confidence: Viviani joined the household in 1639 and Torricelli in 1641 (MacTutor); the month here orders the stop and the day is defaulted. The pendulum escapement drawing is attested; no working clock was built in his lifetime. Milton's visit is reported only by Milton himself in Areopagitica (1644), six years after the fact, and is not corroborated in Galileo's correspondence: tradition, not document.
stops.campa: Vincenzo Viviani, seventeen years old, comes to the house in 1639 as amanuensis and stays. Evangelista Torricelli arrives in 1641 for the last three months. Galileo, blind, dictates further additions to the Discorsi, argues by letter about the libration of the moon, and works with his son Vincenzio on an escapement that would let a swinging weight drive a clock train. The drawing gets made. The clock does not get built. An English traveller, John Milton, will write six years later that he saw him here, a prisoner of the Inquisition.
suggested_refs: John Milton, Areopagitica (1644), on visiting the famous Galileo grown old, a prisoner to the Inquisition
The Galileo-Viviani drawing of the pendulum escapement, Museo Galileo

stops.name: Villa Il Gioiello: four in the morning
stops.date_confidence: Death attested to 8 January 1642 (Museo Galileo). The hour, the two months of slow fever and palpitations, and the presence of Viviani and Torricelli at the bedside all come from Viviani's Racconto istorico, written twelve years later, and are his testimony rather than an independent record.
stops.campa: Two months of slow fever and palpitations of the heart, and on the eighth of January, at about four in the morning, he dies in the house he has not been permitted to leave for eight years. Viviani, twenty, and Torricelli are with him. He is seventy-seven, blind for the last four years, and still formally a prisoner of the Holy Office: the sentence has never been lifted and the Dialogue is still on the Index. The account of the last hours is Viviani's, written down twelve years afterward for a life of his teacher that the Grand Duke commissioned and then did not print.
suggested_refs: Viviani, Racconto istorico della vita di Galileo, composed 1654, first printed 1717

stops.name: Santa Croce, Florence: the unmarked corner
stops.date_confidence: Burial attested to 9 January 1642, and the blocking of the planned Medici monument is attested by the Museo Galileo. The description of the original grave as an unconsecrated box beneath the bell tower comes from the English Wikipedia article on Galileo's middle finger; the precise room is described variously in the sources and is not adjudicated.
stops.campa: Ferdinando II intends a monument in the nave of the Franciscan basilica and a public funeral oration for him. Rome lets it be known, through the Florentine inquisitor, that a man dead under sentence for vehement suspicion of heresy is not to be honoured in that manner, and that the Grand Duke might consider how such a thing would look. The body goes instead into a small space off the novices' chapel, beneath the bell tower, with no ceremony and no inscription over it.
suggested_refs: Museo Galileo, Galilean iconography and relics (catalogue.museogalileo.it/section/GalileanIconographyRelics.html)
sources: Museo Galileo, iconography and relics page

stops.name: Santa Croce, Florence: the tomb of 1737
stops.date_confidence: Transfer attested to 12 March 1737, financed from funds Vincenzo Viviani had left for the purpose. Three fingers and a tooth are named by the Museo Galileo; the fifth lumbar vertebra, given to the University of Padua by Domenico Thiene in 1823, is named by English Wikipedia, and the Museo Galileo's silence about it is a limit of its own holdings rather than a contradiction. Viviani's own remains were moved into the new grave. The tradition that Maria Celeste was reinterred alongside him is not supported by either source reached and is left flagged.
stops.campa: On the twelfth of March the coffin is opened and the remains carried into the nave, into the monument Vincenzo Viviani had left money to build and had not lived to see finished. The general prohibition on books teaching the motion of the earth still has twenty-one years to run. During the transfer five things are taken from the body and kept: three fingers, a tooth, and the fifth lumbar vertebra. The middle finger of the right hand stands upright under glass in a museum a few streets away; the vertebra went to Padua in 1823.
suggested_refs: Galileo's middle finger, Museo Galileo, Palazzo Castellani, inventory 2432
The fifth lumbar vertebra, University of Padua, donated by Domenico Thiene in 1823
sources: Museo Galileo, iconography and relics page
